title: Count it all joy (James 1:1–8)
hookLine: trials produce patience; ask God for wisdom, who gives generously

cards: New letter, new voice. Paul wrote long, winding sentences. The letter of James is short and blunt, more like a book of proverbs than an argument.
It's written to "the twelve tribes which are scattered abroad", believers living far from home. Tradition says the writer is James, the brother of Jesus, who led the church in Jerusalem.
Churches hear that word brother differently. Protestants often take it plainly, a younger brother.
Catholic tradition often speaks of a cousin or close relative, and Orthodox tradition of a son of Joseph by an earlier marriage. Either way, his very first instruction sounds upside down.

teach.h: COUNT IT JOY: A DECISION, NOT A MOOD.
teach.b: In the King James Bible: "My brethren, count it all joy when ye fall into divers temptations." Divers means various, and temptations here means trials, tests of every kind. Fall into, like a pit you didn't see.
Count it all joy. Not feel it, count it: a decision about how you'll book the thing, not a mood. Why?
"Knowing this, that the trying of your faith worketh patience." The word for trying means a test that proves what's genuine. And patience here is a strong word: endurance, the strength to keep going.
Let it finish its work, James says, so you'll be whole, lacking nothing. And if you're in the middle of a trial and don't know what to do?
"If any of you lack wisdom, let him ask of God, that giveth to all men liberally, and upbraideth not; and it shall be given him." Upbraideth not.

teach.h: ASK: GOD GIVES AND DOESN'T SCOLD.
teach.b: In James's picture, God doesn't scold the one who asks. No sigh, no eye roll, no you should know this by now. Just generosity.
One condition: ask in faith, without wavering, because the one who wavers "is like a wave of the sea driven with the wind and tossed."
Such a person, he says, is double minded, literally double-souled.
Not simply someone with questions. Someone pulled two ways at once, asking God for wisdom while planning not to listen.

how: Christians facing a decision sometimes pray the words of James 1:5, asking God for wisdom, and study groups often read the letter of James as a practical guide to everyday faith.

waiting quietly for someone else to act
the strength to keep going under trials

games.q: you're in the middle of a hard trial and you don't know what to do. what does James say?
o: work it out alone so you don't bother God.
ask God for wisdom, who gives generously.
wait for the trial to pass.
games.why: "If any of you lack wisdom, let him ask of God, that giveth to all men liberally, and upbraideth not."

practice: Bring to mind one thing you're facing where you honestly don't know what to do, a decision at work, a relationship, a choice about money or health, and name it plainly.

If you pray, ask God for wisdom about it in your own words; if you don't, sit with the question openly, as if an answer could come. Notice whether one part of you is asking while another part has already decided.

wordCard.voice: Endurance. James's strong word for patience: the strength trials build, so that letting it finish its work leaves you whole, lacking nothing.

orig.note: Greek: double-souled, double minded. James uses it again in 4:8.

carryVoice: Your line: ask for wisdom. The giver doesn't scold. Day six hundred sixty-nine, done.
